newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CALLS FOR RETHINK ON POLICE BOARD SCRAPPING
The Council for Civil Liberties wants the New South Wales government to review its decision to abolish the Police Board.
Council President John Marsden says the decision to sack the board requires further consideration and public debate.

Mr Marsden says while he's not questioning the integrity or capabilities of the Police Commissioner, there is an inherent danger in vesting virtually unfettered power in an individual in this position.
CASE AGAINST HOLLOWAY DISCHARGED

A child sex charge against a former Australian Ambassador to Cambodia has been thrown out of the A.C.T. Magistrates Court. In discharging the case against 53 year-old John Scott Holloway, Magistrate Michael Soames said he had serious doubts about the credibility of the complainant, a 16 year-old Cambodian boy.
The teenager claimed he'd had two sexual encounters with Mr Holloway in Phnom Penh in 1994.

Outside the Court, Mr Holloway has told reporters the Child Sex Tourism Act, under which he was charged, provided a powerful weapon to people with various agendas to make allegations against Australian officials.
SKASE CHASE ON AGAIN
The Christopher Skase chase may be on again....following the Federal Government's approval of extra funding for the pursuit of the assets of the failed businessman.
Last month the Inspector-General for Bankruptcy rejected an application by bankruptcy trustee, Max Donnelly, for further public funding .. saying there was no reasonable chance of success.
The Government has since invited Mr Donnelly to make a fresh application.
Attorney-General Daryl Williams says there are possible avenues to recover assets from Mr Skase .. and he's approved what he says are modest funds to pursue the matter.
Mr Williams if the next step proves fruitful, substantial further funding could be provided .. but there's no guarantee of success.
FIRST TITLE OF LAND COMPLEMENTING NATIVE TITLE ACT
The first title of land granted in Australia to complement the Native Title Act has been handed to traditional landowners in Perth.
The Indigenous Land Corporation has bought the former West Swan Primary School in Henley Brook on Perth's eastern outskirts for three-hundred-thousand dollars.
The Corporation was established last year to assist indigenous people acquire land following the High Court's recognition of Native Title.
Its aim is to help dispossess indigenous people who cannot benefit from Native Title or other land rights legislation.
Corporation chairman, David Ross, has described it as an historic event for all indigenous people in Australia.
EMPLOYMENT HEARINGS TOLD OF FALLING LITERACY AMONG YOUTH
The National Inquiry into Youth Employment, taking place in Brisbane, has been told the literacy levels of high school students are likely to get worse.
The claim comes in the wake of a national study that found one in three Year Nine students don't have adequate literacy levels.
Representative Karyn Heart told the inquiry, many students start their secondary education without adequate reading skills and quickly fall further behind.
SURVEY SHOWS DOUBLING OF RACIST ABUSE
A Chinese Australian community leader has called on decent people of intervene when they see Asian Australians being abused.
The call follows a survey, by the Chinese Australia Forum, into incidents of abuse.
More than a thousand responses were received, showing a doubling of abusive incidents following the maiden speech in parliament of Independent MP Pauline Hanson.
Forum President Dr Thiam Ang says the survey wasn't aimed at Mrs Hanson, rather, the bitter public debate which followed.
He says political leaders haven't been strong enough in calling for sense in the debate, saying it's up to ordinary people to speak out against racist behaviour.
FEARS CHILD CARE CHANGES WILL AFFECT WORKFORCE MAKEUP
The Institute of Chartered Accountants believes key people could be lost from the Australian workforce if proposed changes to child care go ahead.
A taskforce from the government's Economic Plannning Advisory Commission last night publicly released its report on the A$2.4 billion industry.
It recommends scrapping the various funding methods in favour of a single means-tested benefit to parents.

The Institute's tax director, Ian Langford-Brown, says corporate Australia will be most directly hit by the proposed abolition of fringe benefits tax exemptions for work-based care. -- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
